Logarithm of the odds: the base 10 log of how much more likely the data are if a marker and a disease locus are linked than if they are not; a score of 3 (1,000:1 odds) is the classic threshold for linkage.
Theta; the proportion of meioses in which two loci are separated by crossing over, from 0 (completely linked) to 0.5 (unlinked).
Unit of genetic distance equal to 1 percent recombination; on average about 1 megabase of DNA in humans.
Nonrandom association of alleles at nearby loci across a population, so that they are inherited together more often than chance predicts; the basis of association mapping.
Describes alleles that two relatives carry because both inherited them from the same ancestor; full siblings share about half their genome this way.
A linkage method that tests whether pairs of affected siblings share a genome region more often than the 50 percent expected by chance.
Spurious association that arises when cases and controls differ in ancestry rather than in disease status; the main weakness of case-control designs.
The strict p value threshold used to call an association real after testing the whole genome; 5 × 10 to the minus 8 for common-variant studies today.
CNV; a deletion or duplication of a DNA segment ranging from a few base pairs to millions; rare and de novo CNVs contribute to autism and schizophrenia risk.
A case with the same phenotype as a genetic disorder but caused by something other than the gene under study; one reason psychiatric disorders are not simply Mendelian.
The APOE allele on chromosome 19 that raises the risk of late-onset Alzheimer disease; it raises risk without determining illness, and its status now guides anti-amyloid treatment.
PS-1 on chromosome 14 and PS-2 on chromosome 1; with APP, the genes whose dominant mutations cause familial early-onset Alzheimer disease.
A genetic change present in a child but in neither parent; de novo variants confer substantial risk in a minority of autism cases.
Expression of a gene that depends on which parent it came from; in 15q11-13 a maternal defect gives Angelman syndrome and a paternal one Prader-Willi syndrome.
